translations.text: By the same author, Mar Abdisho: On spiritual contemplation, which draws the mind, under the yoke of prayer, above the activity of the senses,
and above their thoughts and their perceptions of sensible things; and on the fiery movement that transforms the soul into its own likeness.
Whenever this contemplation draws the mind toward itself—those, then, whom the grace of God has enabled to prosper,
who have diligently practiced virtuous deeds and purified the chamber of their hearts of passions, desire, and envy,
and anger, slander, and pride, the mother and nurse of all evils,
and have acquired purity of soul and clarity of mind, and because of their love for our Lord Christ
have already become holy temples of God Most High, the King of all ages, according to the word of the prophet who said:
“You are temples of the Lord, if you make your ways and deeds good before him”—
and the power of that treasure of life laid up within them has been revealed to them,
that is, the Holy Spirit whom they received through holy baptism in their new birth, and their mind has acquired holy [?],
which examines the height and depth of all natures, whether we speak of those perceived by the senses or those perceived by the mind.
Whenever they approach prayer and divine worship,
to minister in the order of the spiritual priesthood in that inner Holy of Holies, a fiery movement spreads through their soul.
This gives off fragrance, and an indescribably sweet scent comes forth from it. When the soul breathes it in,
the soul that has been found worthy of this rises from mortality to life and comes out of darkness into light.
And from ignorance it draws near to the knowledge of truth, and from conjecture to certainty through experience,
and from seeing things perceived by the senses to seeing things perceived by the mind,
and from the turmoil of this world's distractions to awareness of the new world.
And the soul is transformed from its natural condition into a likeness that is above its nature.
And from its former condition, in which until now it was subject to passions in its thoughts,
it draws near to freedom from passions in its thoughts through this fiery movement.
For, as though with strong wine, the mind becomes intoxicated and filled with wonder at the sight of that fiery movement through which it undergoes transformation,
through the sweet fragrance of that holy inhalation. Therefore this fiery movement of which I have spoken
is the spiritual key that opens before the mind the inner door of the heart,
and shows it that spiritual place where our Lord Christ dwells within us, in the hidden recess of our heart.
According to the words of the godly Paul, who said, as he urged us toward knowledge of this exalted gift:
“Examine yourselves,” he says, “to see whether you stand in the faith. Test yourselves.
“Or do you not recognize,” he says, “that Jesus Christ is in you? Otherwise, you have failed the test.”
For wherever the Lord Christ dwells, his Spirit is also there, according to the apostle Paul.
And where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is also freedom from the passions. And wherever there are people freed
from the passions, there the kingdom, tranquility, and peace reign, together with joy in the Holy Spirit.
And because of the intensity of the joy and gladness of the heart, a person does not know how to control his senses.
For a person cannot endure the working of this fiery stirring.
Therefore, as soon as this [?] stirring spreads through the soul, a person immediately falls to the ground,
and eats the dust upon it as though it were bread, because of the fervor of divine love and the flame and burning of its heat.
Blessed is the person who has been found worthy of this visitation, and the mortal whose mind’s palate has tasted
some of that sweet delight arising from that fiery stirring, which is tasted in the movements of the soul,
through the merciful compassion of Christ our Lord. And through the working of this divine stirring, when it continues for some time,
then, little by little, spiritual contemplation dawns in the soul like a cloud, concerning the vision and understanding of the worlds that have existed and those that are to come.
And [?], like the son of Amram on the mountaintop, so the face of the mind becomes radiant with the light of its vision.
It draws the intellect to itself, away from the vision and understanding of all objects of knowledge.
And no awareness of anything else remains in the intellect, except the vision and understanding of it.
And the person’s heart is [?] with all this through that holy light of the vision of this contemplation, until the intellect no longer even sees or distinguishes itself.
For all the movements of its spiritual nature take on the likeness of that light at that time. There is no [?] there,
no reflection on anything, no thought or deliberation, no movements, not even fleeting impulses,
but only amazement at God and wonder that cannot be expressed.
Blessed is anyone who has been found worthy of this gift, whose effects cannot be expressed by a tongue of flesh.
For mysteries and revelations are disclosed there, which one mind can receive spiritually from another mind,
since the tongue of flesh has no power to express them.
For the fathers say that in the vision of this holy contemplation:
A person is made worthy to enter that realm of spirituality through the visitation of the vision of this contemplation.
It comes to a person between the level of the soul and the realm of perfection.
For below it is the realm of the soul, where sacrifices and prayers are offered.
But from this visitation upward is the realm of perfection,
where neither sacrifices nor prayers are offered.
Instead, the mysteries and revelations of the new world are revealed there to the spiritual mind.
Therefore, this is the indication and the reliable knowledge by which a person understands:
when someone perceives it, they know that they have already reached the true realm of the soul.
For as long as your mind has not yet reached the vision of this contemplation, recognize within yourself
that in your way of life you stand below the realm of clarity. Struggle against your thoughts with all the strength you have,
and cultivate vigil, fasting, prayer, abstinence, and study of the divine Scriptures, through which you can be raised
to the realm of clarity. For a person rises from the bodily order to purity,
and from purity is lifted to the level of the soul,
and from the level of the soul, in turn, to the perception and vision of this wonderful visitation,
and from the vision of this to entry into that realm of perfection, to serve as a priest in the innermost Holy of Holies,
where the true high priest, our Lord Jesus Christ, is. For there, there is not one light and another light,
nor one image and another image, nor one perception and another perception, but one light, one perception, and one image.
This is the glorious vision of our Savior. May he, in his compassion, make everyone who is of his flesh and of his bones worthy
to enjoy these glorious mysteries—here, in a mystical way, and there beyond, truly, in their actual reality. Amen.
By the same author: On the prayer that occurs in the mind in the realm of clarity, and against those who say that the mind’s vision has an image and a form
when it reaches the realm above clarity; and what the mind’s vision is like in the realm of purity;
and how, when it reaches the realm of clarity, God has no image or form,
since the vision of him is above images and forms. For although in the discourse preceding this one we spoke
about the spiritual contemplation that comes to the mind as a visitation between clarity and the realm of perfection,
nevertheless, it seemed good to me now to speak also about the manner and order of prayer in the realm of clarity.
that clarity comes to the mind. For once the mind has reached clarity, there is no time when it is not praying.
Yet its prayer has a different form from the prayer it offers in the realm of purity.
This is the true prayer that the mind offers in the realm of clarity:
namely, the meanings of the Holy Scriptures, and the mysteries and revelations found in the contemplation of bodily things.
These continually hold the understanding in amazement, in wonder at the depth of the wisdom of the Lord of all that is hidden in them.
This wisdom draws the understanding toward itself, away from all the things performed bodily to satisfy the will of God.
As the apostle said, “He determined the times by his command and established the boundaries of human habitation.”
And, continuing, he said, “So that they might seek God and search for him, and find him through his creatures.”
And again, “The hidden things of God, from the foundations of the world, are seen by his creatures through his works, through understanding [?],
and his eternal power and divinity.” Thus the prayer of the understanding in that realm of clarity has one form, as I have already said.
For there are no prayers and sacrifices there, in that exalted realm, free from the turmoil of the passions, nor supplications and petitions concerning past transgressions.
Nor is there even any remembrance of outward practices, those that are brought to perfection in the realm of purity,
and whose remembrance is continually stirred in the understanding. Rather, all these things
and others like them cease from the mind in the realm of clarity, and their remembrance disappears from the awareness of the understanding.
It is constantly stirred by things that surpass these and are more excellent, in wonder at the creative work of God, who is wise in everything.
For, as I said above, the prayer of the understanding has one form when it has been raised to the realm of clarity:
namely, contemplation and the delightful gaze of spiritual knowledge, which is concealed and hidden in this whole creation. For just as blessed Moses,
when he stood within the thick cloud for the span of six days, during which creation was created by the wise Creator,
had no outward prayer, but only spiritual gazing and contemplation of the creatures of God, the Lord of all,
and communion and conversation with the majesty of that exalted and glorious one, whose name is holy and whose dwelling is holy,
so, in this same way, the understanding that has reached clarity through diligence in its godly practices
has, from that point onward, no gaze or vision of anything else,
apart from one delightful gaze upon the things fashioned by God, the wise Maker.
And this is what the prophet said: “A human being ate bread.”
That is, the spiritual meaning concealed and hidden in the works of God.
And it is perceived and known only by a pure mind that has reached serenity.
In this place the mind is filled with boundless joy and inexpressible gladness. And peace and harmony
and harmony reign over all the [?] and parts of the soul.
And from this a person acquires true love and affection for all people.
He shares their suffering and grieves for them, considering what they are deprived of through the pleasure of lustful impulses.
Therefore, because there are many who openly argue against them, saying that even in the state of serenity there are prayers, sacrifices, sighs, and supplications for former transgressions,
although they do not know what they are saying or what they are arguing about,
I myself want to explain clearly how and in what
order there is a place for prayers to be offered, and for petitions and supplications concerning former transgressions,
and where the memory of them is stirred in the soul, and they awaken it to the labors of repentance.
Now, when a person has left this world with a discerning resolve arising from the fear of God,
and has entered this holy order of solitary life, and has now begun on the path of virtues [?],
and his foot has already stepped into the stage of bodily practice, then he begins to dig deep and lay a foundation for his way of life:
that is, unceasing labors [?] of every kind, those performed through the body.
Except [?] of every kind, those performed through the body.
For the memory of the former transgressions he committed constantly pricks him.
And he cannot rest or grow neglectful of outward labors [?],
which are carried out through the body to satisfy God's will [?]. For the fire of the natural seeds
is also stirred within him here. And the more it flares up in his heart, the more he increases his labors [?] and multiplies his acts of charity.
And he develops his virtue in many different ways: through mercy toward the poor and unfortunate,
through compassion for the needy, through sympathy for the distressed and afflicted,
through welcoming strangers, through washing the feet of the weary, through visiting the sick,
through caring for those in pain, together with the other virtues resembling these.
He struggles and labors so that all those commandments that our Lord spoke in the Gospel to those on his right:
“I was sick and you visited me, and I was naked and you clothed me.”
And I was a stranger, and you welcomed me. I was in prison, and you came to me.
Along with the rest, so that, step by step, they may be found in their fullness in the person who has begun this holy path.
Through all these things, and others that we have not mentioned, the soul is purified of its passions.
I mean desire and anger, which assists it. So when the soul has been purified of these,
so that they are not stirred in a contrary way and do not act toward the left, but act according to their natural order,
then, from that very point, the soul becomes a fountain of prayers, petitions, and supplications to God.
From this it acquires purity. And when it has been purified and has now become established in its natural order,
it is continually seen as resembling the color of sapphire [?] and of the sky. And all its prayers
all rise in the heart like clouds of incense from fire, from fire.
They purify and cleanse the soul, like iron that enters the fire, which purges all the rust from it.
So too with the soul: together with the activity of those natural seeds that work within it,
its prayers purify it and bring it near to the place of serenity.
In the place of serenity, all the movements of prayer cease, as I explained above.
For there the soul has no recollection of any of its former transgressions that would press it to offer prayers and supplications.
Instead, the peace that surpasses all understanding and tranquility dwell in all the movements of the soul and the mind.
The mind remembers nothing except wonder at the wisdom of God, which is hidden in the natures and things of creation.
For understanding of God's judgment and providence also shines continually within the soul and draws it toward itself,
like a lodestone that draws particles of iron toward itself.
It does not allow the soul to turn to prayer or to perform any other activity.
Instead, it continually draws the soul into wonder at the compassion of God, the Lord of all.
In wonder and amazement at such things, all the movements of prayer cease and remain [?] inactive.
For a person offers prayers for these reasons: either one prays because of failings into which one has previously fallen,
or because of bodily illness, or because of a lack of necessary things, or for deliverance from one's passions,
which are continually stirred within one and sting one with the distress they cause,
or for freedom and deliverance from the tyrannical demons that wage war against us, or because of the injuries inflicted on us by others.
Or so that things may go well for us, along with other things like these, which there is no need to mention in full.
For all these reasons that I have mentioned, then, we offer prayer to God.
[?] that he may grant us escape and deliverance from them, and give us the help of his mercy, so that we may be blameless before him.
In short, it is because of these things, and because we remember them, that we offer supplication to God.
“Sacrifices and offerings are where sin is practiced,” said one of the saints.
Therefore, when the intellect has already reached the realm of clarity and escaped the assault of the passions,
and has been freed from the disturbance caused by sin, the remembrance of all these things mentioned above ceases within it.
For in the realm of clarity it is above the realm of the passions and their activity.
From then on, the mind has only one prayer there: for the return of people held captive by error,
that they may turn from wickedness to virtue [?], and from ignorance to knowledge of the truth.
Apart from this one prayer, it has no other, unless it is vision [?] and wonder at the richly varied wisdom of God,
which is hidden in the natures of created things. I am not speaking here of partial clarity,
but of complete clarity. For there is a clarity that is partial,
that is partial, and there is one that is perfect, in which the intellect is enveloped in clouds of crystalline light,
like that stammerer, the son of Amram, beloved by God, on the summit of the mountain for six days.
For whenever the intellect reaches the measure of true clarity,
it is continually clothed in contemplation resembling the light of crystal.
This is the realm in which spiritual beings are seen in their own nature,
those whose utterances are burning, blazing fire.
For this is the realm in which spiritual beings spiritually proclaim
the threefold “Holy” to the hidden and concealed One who dwells in majestic light, which no one can approach [?].
As the prophet Isaiah, son of Amoz, said: “I saw the Lord seated on a high and exalted throne,
and the splendor of his glory filled his temple. Seraphim stood above him,
each of them with six wings. They flew and soared without ceasing,
and called to one another, saying, ‘Holy, holy, holy is the Lord Almighty; the earth is full of his praises.’”
And from this realm of serenity the mind is raised to the realm of spirituality, where its vision has neither likeness nor shape.
For it is entirely enveloped in a single vision of incomparable light. Yet there are many who babble with [?] knowledge and say:
“From serenity upward, the mind’s vision has likeness and shape,” although they do not know what
they are saying. For how could this possibly be so?
At that time the mind itself does not know, and cannot distinguish its own self from the glory of that incomparable light,
in which its spirituality is absorbed. And if this is true, how can these people say
that the mind’s vision [?] has likeness and shape from serenity upward?
For just as God has neither likeness nor shape, even though shapes are attributed to him in the Scriptures,
through which he displayed his revelations and made himself known to us, nevertheless all these are outside the nature of his being.
For the nature of his being in no way resembles fire or the light of the sun,
or air, or any of the other elements, or the material substances derived from them.
For the nature of his being is exalted above all the shapes, likenesses, and compounds in this creation of ours.
For his nature is [?] even than fire, light, and air,
so that, compared with that glorious nature of the Lord of all, these are [?] and heavy bodies.
Therefore he has no likeness in even one of the things visible in our creation.
The same is true of the mind, the image of God,
when it reaches the realm of perfection and the exalted measure of spirituality.
For every prayer has [?] imprinted in it.
And just as God, the [?], has neither likeness nor shape, neither does the mind, his image, when it reaches the realm—
the realm of perfection. There, neither the mind itself nor its vision has likeness or shape.
For when its spirituality is absorbed in that hidden glory of the contemplation of the Holy Trinity,
no one can distinguish its nature there from that holy light, nor does it have shapes or likenesses there.
Those who, by the grace of our Lord, have been found worthy understand what I am saying:
worthy to enter that realm of perfection. And they know that everything I have said is true
and contains no falsehood, since no one attains this through writings and hearsay.
Apart from the experience of individual beings, the mind has no vision of anything there at all, except the glorious vision of our Savior:
that vision which is above the senses and above perceptible forms and images.
Therefore, what, then, does this very thing mean for Mar Isaac, illustrious among the saints? [?]
“Those,” he says, “who speak of seeing our Savior in this world in a manner other than contemplation
are companions of those who speak of enjoying his kingdom in the world to come in a sensory way,
with the use of material elements and the solidity of individual beings.” He goes on afterward to say:
“Both,” he says, “have strayed from the truth, since his brothers, too, become like him.”
For when our Lord Christ is revealed to the minds of the saints in the realm above serenity,
his glorious appearance has neither an image nor a composite form. Blessed, my brothers, is whoever has been found worthy to see
our Lord Christ in this vision of which I have spoken, and has died to the world and all its delights.
For the appearance of our Savior—the appearance in which he now exists after his resurrection from the dead—
cannot be expressed or grasped by the human mind. And why do I say human beings,
when even spiritual beings cannot grasp or explain his appearance,
and cannot comprehend or gaze upon that wondrous, incomparable glory in which our Lord rose from the tomb?
And if the sight of the holy angels is dazzled by his glory, and they cannot comprehend that greatness [?],
how can anyone say that our human mind can depict and compose
that exalted and inexpressible glory with which our Lord clothed himself at the resurrection from the dead?
Therefore, in the realms of spirituality, the mind has no vision of anything:
neither contemplation of bodies nor of what is bodiless, neither of judgment nor of providence.
Nor, in any way, is a conception of anything that exists cast into the mind,
except the vision of our Savior himself, which makes all spiritual beings stand in amazement.
Truly, my brothers, I am not lying: whenever even the memory of that glorious vision
rises in my mind, all the movements of the body, together with those of the soul, are swallowed up in inexpressible amazement,
and no thought at all stirs in my soul apart from wonder at him. And if among the lowly [?]—15—
the lowly and weak like me, this happens merely from remembering his greatness.
To the strong and to those who are perfect, [?] who continually delight in the glorious vision of our Savior.
What can anyone say except what I said above? For just as in the wondrous realms of the holy angels,
no thought about anything in this world is stirred or flutters within them,
except the remembrance and vision of our Lord himself, so also, for the pure mind, from the realm of serenity upward,
there is no vision or remembrance of anything else, apart from the vision of our Savior himself and the delightful gaze upon him.
And again, just as in the realms of the intelligible and invisible powers there are neither shapes nor images of anything composite,
but their realm is spiritual and they themselves are spiritual, so also, for the pure mind in the realm of spirituality,
its vision has neither an image nor a composite shape. For when the mind reaches that place,
it is like them, and together with them it proclaims holy and exalts that glorious Being.
Just as in the new world there is no shape or image of anything in this world of ours,
because it is above all the shapes, images, and composite things that are here,
so also the vision of the spiritual person has no shape or image of any of the things of this world.
For the mind’s vision of what is there is a pledge of the new world.
And everything revealed to it there belongs to the new world. 16.
As the apostle said, “Now we see, as in a mirror, in a riddle,” the pledge of the glory of the resurrection.
“But then face to face,” when we receive the resurrection in actual reality.
And again he said, “The eye has not seen, and the ear has not heard,
nor has it entered the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him.”
From all these things that the blessed apostle said, it is clear that in the realm of the mind’s spirituality there is no
shape or image of anything composite. And if the hope of chaste solitaries extends only this far,
that even in the realm of spirituality their mind’s vision does not rise above the shapes and images of composite things,
they are more miserable than all other people. But it is not so—far from it! Rather, the opposite is true.
This is what we solitaries await and hope for: that in the realm of spirituality we may see that which,
in its exaltedness, is above the senses of the body and the movements of the soul.
As in the testimony given above, which the apostle spoke for our instruction and teaching:
So that we do not confine the course of our mind to things perceived by the senses and turn away from things that are unseen.
And they are awaited in hope alone [?]. I have said it, and I say it again:
If all our present knowledge of our Lord Christ, and the glorious vision of him that is seen within our hearts, amounts only to an outward form,
then Christ died in vain, and his coming into our world has brought us no benefit.
And his suffering and death on our behalf amount to nothing, if, as—
as with the ancient fathers and prophets, he appears to his holy ones even now in forms and likenesses.
But now it is not so. Rather, ever since our Lord Christ was revealed in a body taken from us, for the salvation and renewal of all rational beings,
the manner of his revelations, both to us and to the invisible powers, has changed.
He no longer appears in composite likenesses, as he did to those people of old,
but rather in a glorious vision, beyond likenesses and forms perceived by the senses.
We do indeed say that we see light there, in that realm of spiritual existence, but it is not like this material light.
And we have spiritual food there, but certainly not like the food here.
And there our mind has the sound of the spiritual beings’ praise of holiness, speech, and conversation.
But it is not like the speech we have with one another.
For the speech heard there by the mind is subtle, and our senses cannot receive it.
Therefore, the tongue of flesh cannot speak about or describe what is revealed there to the mind,
whether someone calls it seeing or hearing.
As the apostle said when admonishing the Corinthians about this, speaking as though in the person of someone else:
“Whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows. He was caught up into Paradise
and heard words that cannot be spoken, which a human being is not permitted to utter.”
Through these words he clearly showed that the things cannot be put into the structure of language
that are revealed to the mind at the level of perfection.
For how could this be, when someone does not know whether he is in the body or outside the body, according to the testimony of the divine apostle?
Therefore, none of the mysteries and revelations disclosed to the mind from the realm of clarity and above can be put into words,
as can the other revelations, from clarity and below.
And even when the mysteries and revelations of that realm are disclosed, the mind cannot put them into composite forms.
How, then, do so many speculate and say that the understanding's vision has a form in the realm above clarity,
and that the faint whispers of the spiritual beings' praise of holiness are heard there?
For just as God has no form, as I said above,
so neither does what is revealed to the understanding there have a form of any kind,
since all composite forms, shapes, images, and numbers belong to clarity and the levels below it.
Therefore, however much the mind struggles to raise its vision above composite forms and images, it cannot do so in the realm extending from clarity downward.
For conflicts and struggles also exist in that realm, and there they have room to wage war against the mind.
For the understanding's vision also has images and shapes as long as its activity remains there.
But from clarity upward, it has risen above all shapes, images, composite forms, and numbers.
There is no Satan there, nor any evil encounter,
but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. And if anyone argues about
about this, he has been carried away into error without realizing it.
He has never become familiar with the writings of the spiritual fathers, nor has he personally gained experience of the matter.
He does not understand what clarity is, nor the realm above it.
Indeed, he does not even understand purity, nor purity. Rather, he says whatever happens to occur to him.
This wise man neither knows nor understands even one of these levels:
these levels are arranged like steps and a ladder, by which the mind climbs, advancing step by step on its journey until it reaches the top of that ladder on which the Lord rests,
which is the level of spirituality and the limit of the mind's course [?]. For the seal and the true stamp
is clarity of understanding. That is, as long as a person's way of life remains below clarity,
the seal has not yet been placed on the record of his virtues.
For sometimes he works with God like a hired worker, looking every day for payment for his labors,
and sometimes like a slave, looking for release and freedom from slavery.
But it is not like this in the realm of clarity. Rather, it is the opposite.
For when a person reaches the realm of clarity, he is freed from the designation of slavery and hired service [?].
And he is enrolled among the adopted sons and becomes an heir of God and a fellow heir with Jesus Christ.
He no longer works with God as a slave or a hired worker, but as a son with his father. He is stamped with the seal of the Spirit
and given authority over his Father's treasures. Fear and anxiety are removed from him, and he gains the confidence of sons,
so that from that very place he may call God Father, as the apostle said to the Romans who believed in our Lord:
“You did not receive a spirit of slavery leading back to fear,
but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, through whom we cry, ‘Abba, our Father.’
The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God. And if children, then also heirs—
heirs of God and fellow heirs with Jesus Christ.” Therefore, once he has already been raised to the realm of clarity
and enrolled among the adopted sons, he continually shares with God in the revelation of his mysteries.
From then on he sees everything spiritually and hears from that very place.
His worship and the hallowing expressed in his song are continually shared with the spiritual beings.
Blessed is the person who has attained this gift and this confidence,
who has seen that glorious vision with the eyes of his mind and heard with the ears of his heart that subtle sound
which is uttered to the spiritual person beyond clarity. Truly, my brothers, believe me in what I tell you:
whenever the mind hears the sound of the spiritual beings with its spiritual ears,
all its activity is beyond the bodily senses, and the body's movements are silent and still, as in sleep,
because of the delight it receives from the hallowing offered by the spiritual beings. And while the body sleeps, the movements of the mind flutter in wakefulness—
they flutter, for they have no rest from worship alongside the spiritual beings.
For this reason, night and day are alike to the mind that has been deemed worthy of this gift through the grace of our Lord.
To him be glory from all the rational beings he created and made participants in his glory, those above and those below. Amen.
Again by the same author: On the activity of the movements that dawn in the mind at the time of prayer:
which are compound, which are simple, and which are without limit and [?].
At the time of prayer, the soul is like a ship standing in the heart of the sea.
The mind stands over the ship like a helmsman, while the movements that guide the ship are like winds.
And just as not all the winds that blow are suitable for the ship's voyage.
So too with the movements stirred in the soul during prayer:
not all of them are suitable for the ship’s voyage, so that it may reach the harbor without danger, sheltered from the waves.
Some are, and some are not, because some imprint composition and form upon the soul.
These hinder the voyage of the ship whose pilot is the mind, toward the harbor at which its desire is directed.
But some of the movements stirred in the soul during prayer are simple.
These are gentle winds that guide the soul’s ship above the [?],
toward the harbor filled with great rest. There are also other movements which, during prayer, in light
shine forth. These are called limitless. They are neither composite nor simple,
but [?] limit, as I said above. For simple movements are not necessarily also limitless.
For the holy angels and the natures of our souls are also simple,
but they are certainly not also limitless. They are simple, yet subject to a limit.
For there is only One who is limitless in every respect, and all movements concerning him are limitless, as the prophet said:
“There is no limit to his understanding.” Composite movements, however, are these:
all the thoughts stirred in the soul through the bodily senses—these are composite.
They impede the soul’s journey during prayer.
For even if they are beneficial, nevertheless, during prayer they are harmful to the soul.
This is because, during prayer, simple movements lead the soul upward by stages toward those that are limitless.
Simple movements are these: the hidden spiritual knowledge concealed in the natures of created things;
wonderful insights concerning contemplation without bodily form; and those that arise from contemplation of judgment and providence.
All these movements occur during prayer and are simple.
Therefore, whenever they are revealed to the understanding during prayer, they sweeten the mind’s palate like a honeycomb.
With their warmth they set ablaze all the powers of the soul together with those of the body. And tears that do not fall from a person’s eyes
—a person’s [?]—when these movements are stirred in his understanding,
not from suffering or sorrow over sins, but rather from joy and delight,
and wonder at God’s creative power, his mercy, and his providential care for all: how abundantly his mercy is poured out upon us human beings!
And how great our ingratitude toward him is, and how, when we did not exist and could not even bring ourselves into being,
he in his compassion brought us into existence and enabled us to live well,
although he knew our ingratitude and wickedness very well before he created us. And when we sinned and angered him by our various evil deeds,
he, in his fatherly love, did not withhold from us the gifts of his care and provision for us.
And how, when our nature had reached the point of despair, he sent his beloved Son, our Lord Jesus,
and handed him over to the suffering of death [?] on our behalf, to redeem us who were stained by sin; and he tasted [?] and bitter things for our sake,
enough to neutralize in us the venom of the serpent that killed us in Eden.
And how, after all the wickedness and blasphemies we commit against him, he, in his indescribable grace,
prepared for us another world filled with every good thing and ordained for us the gift of resurrection,
through which we are raised above the sufferings of mortality and become incorruptible and immortal,
no longer liable to turn aside, to suffer, or to be in need; and we are continually raised up with him through understanding his mysteries
and through the glorious vision of him. And so, through remembering all these things,
the movements of the mind reach out from the realm of composite things toward those movements that have no limit,
which are wonder at the new world and the vision [?] of the contemplation of the Holy Trinity.
For when the understanding’s vision mingles with that light of the glorious Trinity, all its movements become limitless. For there is no one
among those who see and know who can distinguish the mind itself from the vision of that glorious light of the Holy Trinity that appears.
For all the inner chambers of the heart are filled with that blessed light.
There is no image distinct from another image there, nor shapes, composite things, numbers, or colors.
Rather, there is one light in singleness of vision [?], which is not differentiated by shapes or images.
But I also tell you this: there, at that moment, there is no movement distinct from another movement,
nor thought distinct from another thought, nor reflection distinct from another reflection, but wonder alone,
which is above all our reflections, movements, and thoughts. It is the pledge of the good things to come,
which have been prepared through the mediation of our Lord Jesus Christ for the human race—that is, for all rational beings—
out of the abundant mercy of that worshipful Father, who created us when we did not exist and gave us a share in the knowledge of his glory,
so that we might exist without end like him and delight in his glory. May he, in his compassion, make us all worthy of the vision of him.
to his glorious vision—here as a pledge, and there in reality. Amen.
By the same author, again, from the Book of Questions: How the Spirit who works in us is recognized.
And how his power is revealed, and what the sign of the Spirit is when he displays his activity in us.
The first sign of the effective working of the Spirit's visitation is this:
The thought of love for God burns like fire in a person's heart.
From this are born in his heart hatred of the world, renunciation, love of living as a stranger, and asceticism,
which is the mother and nurturer of all the virtues.
The second sign, my brother, by which you perceive that the Spirit you received at baptism is at work,
is this: true humility is born in your soul. I do not mean bodily humility, but the true humility that comes from the soul.
With this humility, when great and wonderful things are done for a person by the Spirit who dwells in him,
he considers himself dust and ashes, a worm and not a human being.
In his eyes, all people are regarded as great and holy,
with no distinction in his mind between good and evil people, or between the righteous and sinners.
From humility are born in the soul gentleness, lowliness, and patient endurance of afflictions.
The third sign of the Spirit's activity within you
is compassion, which forms the likeness of God in you.
When your thoughts are occupied with all people, tears pour from your eyes like springs of water.
It is as though all people dwell in your heart, and you embrace and kiss them with love,
while in your thoughts you pour out your kindness upon them all.
When you remember them, your heart burns like fire with the [?] of the Spirit's activity within you.
From this, goodness and kindness are born in your heart,
so that you cannot say anything to anyone, nor does your mind think evil of anyone.
Instead, you do good to all people in thought and deed.
The fourth sign by which you know that the Spirit's visitation is at work within you
is true love, which leaves nothing in your mind except the remembrance of God alone.
which is the spiritual key by which the inner door of the heart is opened, within which Christ our Lord is hidden.
The place where he dwells is spiritual and spacious, and the vision of him is one of indescribable light.
From this love, faith is born—the faith that sees hidden things,
which the mind is not permitted to entrust to paper. The apostle called it the substance of things hoped for,
things that cannot be perceived by bodily eyes, but are clearly perceived by the eyes of the mind in the heart’s inner place.
Now the sign of the five [?] that the Spirit you received at baptism brings about in you is the luminous [?] vision of your mind,
which appears in the firmament of your heart like sapphire and is itself the receiver of the light of the Holy Trinity.
This knowledge stirs you toward the contemplation of things perceived by the senses.
From this, in turn, you are raised to the knowledge of things perceived by the intellect.
From these, in turn, you ascend to revelations and mysteries of judgment and providence.
This ladder raises you and unites you with that holy light of the vision of our Lord Jesus Christ.
From that glorious and holy vision, wonder carries you into that spiritual [?] world whose blessings cannot be described.
From that wonder, an understanding of spiritual speech is born in you, and knowledge of both worlds,
of what has been and what is, and contact with the mysteries of things to come, together with ascent and a holy tasting,
and the subtle utterances of spiritual minds, and joy, exultation, gladness, glory, singing, and praise,
and a song of exaltation, and fellowship with the spiritual ranks, and the vision of the souls of the saints,
and the vision of paradise, and eating from the tree of life, and conversation with the saints who dwell there,
together with other things that cannot be described. These are the signs: when you see them in your soul,
you know that the Holy Spirit whom you received at holy baptism is at work in you.
Questioner: What difference is there between images with real substance
and phantom images? And what passions accompany them?
And how are these images thwarted when they wage war against the mind engaged in spiritual work?
For in the Book of Chapters you mentioned them—these two kinds of images—
but you did not clearly distinguish them. The Solitary: There is a great difference between images with real substance and phantom images.
For some arise from thoughts of sexual immorality, and others from thoughts of vainglory.
Now the images with individual form that arise from vainglory are these:
Those composed by demons in the likeness of angels, which appear as though they had the form of a human being and the wings of a bird;
and other forms resembling a pillar of light or the sphere of the sun.
These images that I have mentioned, then, arise from vainglory and pride. When they attack the soul,
it should take refuge in humility and consider itself dust and ashes and the refuse of all creation.
It should acquire obedience, endurance in afflictions, contempt for itself, and the disposition to be despised in its own eyes.
Through these things, they vanish from the sight of the practicing mind [?], like chaff before the wind.
Now these idol-like images are born from thoughts of sexual immorality
of sexual immorality, and from sadness and anger. That is, demons depict them before the practitioner in the likeness of statues of female idols,
faces that he does not know. Images of animals are also composed before the mind,
as well as the likeness of stones and mountains. Again, these idol-like images appear
as they appeared [?] to certain of the fathers, composed of two natures:
that is, the likeness of a human being and the likeness of an animal together.
[?] Such images are called idol-like images.
And what drives these away from the sight of the practicing mind is
fasting, keeping vigil, prostration, and unceasing prayer of the mind. To put it briefly:
Every thought that composes an image within the heart, when that image has an individual form, is called an image with individual form.
And all thoughts sown within the mind that do not have the form of a person are called idol-like images.
This is the distinction between images with individual form and idol-like images, and these are the remedies for healing each of them.
For vainglory, pride, and arrogance very readily depict and compose images with individual form.
Another letter by the same Mar Abdisho to one of those who loved him, concerning the workings of grace.
Blessed is God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has revealed the mystery of his love in our hearts
and caused the understanding of his grace to dawn in our minds. I have heard about you, O man of God, from
the beloved brothers who came to us, that you have great love for us in our Lord.
And from reading your letter I learned that this is indeed so.
Because of the good testimony about you, I wished to mingle my love with yours.
And I will write to you about the things you asked of our humble self. Know, my lord,
that some of the visions you have experienced are genuine, while others are an appearance full of the deceit and trickery of error.
Since your dwelling is far from you [?], and coming to us is not easy for you,
I wished to explain to you by letter the nature of these experiences.
As for what you said: “At times I stand and look into my soul, and no thought stirs within it, either of righteousness or of its opposite,
but only the mind immersed within itself, without any activity, not even murmuring praise;
rather, rest [?] alone reigns over all the movements of body and soul, so that it finds no pleasure in reading or reciting a psalm.”
The mind alone receives nourishment from within, and the body too is nourished by it. As long as the mind remains in this place, my brother,
this state is far superior to all the changing states of activity that occur in the soul.
Those who have knowledge say that in this state nourishment is secretly given to the mind by the Holy Spirit,
and the body too is nourished by it and has no need of its necessary food. For this immersion in which it is immersed—
in which the mind is immersed in this state—is the very one in which blessed Moses was immersed on Mount Sinai.
As long as you remain in this state, do not trouble yourself about reading or the service of psalms.
Only keep the mind pure. That is, do not leave stillness at all.
If possible, during these days when your mind remains in this state, do not meet anyone.
If possible, do not even listen to the sound of a bird. Instead, enter your inner cell and shut all the doors,
and remain steadfast in what is happening within you. But when this state has passed from you,
a state of active insights follows it. Here, beware of the demon of distraction.
For as long as insights shine within the mind from inside, maintain stillness and the rule of the first state.
But if the mind begins to wander after ideas outside itself, forming images and combining ideas,
set aside the former rule and take up psalmody, reading, and prostrations before the cross.
Stand courageously and firmly, and do not allow the mind to [?] go outside the inner door of the heart,
lest it squander its life in the distraction of thoughts. After this state of insights,
if the mind is kept from the distraction of affections, another state follows: a love of psalms and reading.
And in this way the flame of the psalms and reading blazes within the heart,
so that, if possible, even when someone sits down to eat, the mind is inwardly occupied with the psalms and reading.
The activity of the demon of vainglory accompanies this change.
But examine and see, when you perform the service and read, whether you perform the service out of love for God,
or whether perhaps other images are being formed within him, for whose sake he performs his service and his reading.
Then again, after this change involving the psalms and reading,
another change follows it, if the mind is [?] from thoughts of vainglory.
This is the bursting forth of tears and continual prostration before the cross.
These tears do not come through forcing oneself, nor does the will have control over them.
Rather, fire alone sets the soul ablaze within, while the body outwardly pours out tears.
This change involving these tears is the boundary between purity and clarity.
For they are above the realm of purity and below the realm of clarity.
Nevertheless, they bring the mind into the realm of clarity.
After this activity of these tears, the activity of two contemplations takes place in the mind,
namely, contemplation of judgment and of providence. From the [?] of these, love for humanity arises in the soul,
and continual supplication for their return. For when the mind looks within itself,
it sees everyone in the likeness of the image in which they were created.
Here, in the vision belonging to this change, there is neither sinner nor righteous person, neither slave nor free person,
neither circumcision nor uncircumcision, neither male nor female; rather, Christ is seen as all and in everyone.
After this change, another change follows it: flashes shine out and rise within the heart.
They are like light mingled with fire.
In this change there is a greater activity, and it takes place in the third and fourth senses.
After this activity, another change follows, more excellent than this one.
The activity takes place in the second sense alone, as it hears the sound of a delicate utterance of praise,
which the movements of the body and soul cannot bring into articulate speech.
This transformation and this praise belong to the new world.
It is the pledge of the good things to come.
For this is the working of that Spirit of whom the blessed apostle said that she prays on behalf of the saints.
In this transformation, the cloud of the spiritual cherubim becomes visible to you. You also hear their delicate voices.
When these spread out, your mind is united with them in a song of exaltation. After this praise,
the mind falls silent and is swallowed up in the light of the vision of that lofty and [?] contemplation, like
a fish in the sea. In this transformation, the mind mingles with that activity which makes them one.
For the mind’s light cannot be distinguished from that sea in which it swims.
In this transformation, only the first sense is active.
After this transformation, the following transformation comes next:
fire clothes the person from the sole of his foot to his brain.
When the person looks at himself, he does not see his composite body,
but only the fire in which he is clothed. This is the transformation of which the holy Mar Evagrius spoke
when distinguishing those who possess knowledge from those who do not possess knowledge. For he says this:
“Those who now possess subtle bodies of spirit reigned in the ages that have passed.
But those who are yoked to a laboring body will reign in the ages to come.”
By “subtle bodies” he means the bodies of the saints who have attained this transformation that I have described.
And so that no one may doubt these things, we bring him another testimony, so that he may be more firmly assured of them.
For the blessed Palladius says this about Abba Arsenius:
“While he was [?] in prayer, this transformation came upon him, so that he became entirely like fire.
One of the brothers, a man possessing knowledge, came and saw the old man through the window, entirely like fire.”
The writer testified that this brother was worthy of this vision,
because he was a seer: he saw Abba Arsenius in this transformation. 16.
Transformation. Again, after this transformation, there is another transformation, which cannot be put into writing [?].
Only know that it does happen. Its sign is this: there are no two or three.
Nor is the fourth separate from the fifth. Rather, one expands and the other contracts.
Both receive the same nourishment in this change. Now, in these two changes that I mentioned,
with regard to the activity of the first sense and the fifth, again, after this change,
another change follows it, one of joy. There is also an outpouring of tears in it.
A person does not know the cause of this joy. He knows only that he sees.
But he does not understand why he sees. Here the fourth and third senses are active,
because the activities of these two senses accompany one another.
After this change comes a change involving an outpouring of spiritual speech, which is the activity of the second sense.
Up to this point we have informed you about the workings of grace as far as we were able.
But now, my dear friend, let us speak about the deception of the rebellious ones, which imitates the truth.
First, however, I spoke about the changes in the working of heat.
The demon of insolence begins to produce heat in those engaged in spiritual labor in this way:
its heat begins at the head and descends downward. 16.
A great heaviness presses upon the head, together with disturbance in the head itself, heaviness, and a deep sinking into sleep,
while it is not yet able to sow the seed of its wickedness in him for the time being.
It advises him that during this activity neither reading nor psalms are needed.
If the person obeys it, it increases its heat in this way until it damages the brain.
But if he does not obey its advice and begins reciting psalms and reading, then it descends and causes its heat to break out
around the heart, or in the [?] opposite the heart. This is the sign of its deception:
as soon as its heat begins, lethargy begins in the body,
along with an inner disturbance of thoughts of vainglory, and notions about things that make no sense.
Here distraction of thought gains greater control over the mind. In this change it also produces the fragrance of its deception.
But this is the sign of its fragrance: the more it gives off its scent, the more confusion of thoughts rules in the soul.
It also produces its fragrance from the natural properties of created things, since it has something to which it can be compared.
But the fragrance of grace has no likeness among any of these earthly things that affect sensory perception.
Thus, keeping vigil and prostrating oneself before the cross are required of those who practice the spiritual life until this temptation passes.
Then the enemy moves on to the third group of bodily organs, and begins
and begins to kindle his heat, and with it thoughts of sexual immorality.
This rises as far as the kidneys. The remedy for this temptation is:
fasting, constant vigils, abstaining from drinking water, and also continual walking accompanied by psalm-singing and reading.
One should not sleep lying down,
but sitting or standing on one's feet, for as long as one remains under this temptation.
Now listen also concerning other varieties of apparitions shown by demons.
Whenever, in contemplation, you see an appearance of fire that has a composite form,
know and recognize that this is a snare of the malicious one, with which he wants to catch you and bring you to destruction.
But you, diligent worker, turn your gaze inward, away from the outward form,
and you will find the inside of the visible form full of darkness.
For as soon as the gaze of the discerning person falls upon the form appearing before him,
the falseness of its deception is exposed. But if you see something like a sphere before you,
this too is an apparition produced by demons. Or if it resembles a throne or a chariot,
or a horse of fire—all these, my brother, are demonic deceptions.
In short, everything that appears outside you in these forms is a demonic deception.
The vision of contemplation, then, is simple, and it contains no composite form, whether it is seen inwardly or outwardly.
Demons, however, have no power to enter within and display the forms of their deception.
But if at times you see something within yourself resembling a sphere or a star, do not be alarmed.
For the soul also appears in these different forms. But beware of those things that appear outwardly.
Take care, my brother, and beware also of another form that demons display:
one mingled with light and darkness, which is the activity of the demon of anger.
There is another whose light shines intensely; this is the form of the demon of sexual immorality.
For there is another fiery form, which belongs to the demon of pride.
You can distinguish all these things, my brother, by the indication I give you.
Whenever you see your mind at peace, with tranquility reigning over it,
know that this is the working [?] of grace, with no deception in it.
But if, when you [?] these [?], the contemplation of your soul [?] begins to shrink,
and your heart fills with distress and oppressive thoughts, together with distraction, know that this comes from demons,
along with the other appearances manifested by demons,
which resemble those that come to the soul through grace at the time of prayer.
These things, my beloved, I have outlined for you, as you lovingly requested,
for you in brief. But you, diligent worker, read and understand what is set down before you, and pray for me.
And know, my lord, that if these things come from the right, we should increase our supplication, and let our thoughts be dust.
And if they come from the left, let us cry out with groaning to the one who can raise us [?] from among the dead.
Blessed is the one who has clothed himself in the one who is within him. Blessed too is whoever has been deemed worthy to delight in what is within him.
Whether we know or do not know, let us not call ourselves knowledgeable.
And whether we are sinners or righteous, let us take refuge in the mercies of Christ.
